storySeeds.title: The nursery district of Sagittarius
storySeeds.description: Cold dark cloud (Pipe) → glowing nursery (Lagoon) and its newborn cluster → a slightly older sibling out of its cloud (M21) → the same kind of family 200 Myr on (M23); then the dust window (M24) and the two nurseries of the next arm in (M17, M16). Region about 15° across; compact 5-stop cut: M8 → NGC6530 → M21 → M23 → M24.
storySeeds.note: Follows doc 03 tour U1 and the Astronomical League binocular Messier list; every stop is an AL “easy” or “dark-sky” target except the Pipe (naked-eye/wide-field).

storySeeds.title: Scorpius tail: a family album
storySeeds.description: Start with the ζ Sco pair (foreground orange giant vs member hypergiant twist), then the age ladder NGC 6231 (~4 Myr) → M6 (~50 Myr, with orange BM Sco as timestamp) → M7 (~170 Myr, Ptolemy’s cluster), finishing on an ancient globular (NGC 6397, ~11.5 Gyr) for southern observers.

storySeeds.title: Near and far around Antares
storySeeds.description: Antares and M4 share a field but differ ~10× in distance and ~1000× in age (LINE_OF_SIGHT twist); then M80 (5× farther than M4) and the lopsided/flattened globulars M62 and M19 near the Galactic hub, Shapley’s clue to where the centre lies.

storySeeds.title: A globular from another galaxy
storySeeds.description: Distance/lookback ladder of Sagittarius globulars: M22 (~10,800 ly) → M28 (~17,500 ly; same kind, smaller look) → M54 (~86,000 ly, nucleus of the Sagittarius dwarf galaxy) → twist M55 (nearer, bigger-looking but 8× less massive) → coda M75 in the far halo.

card.question: Can you actually see a cloud where stars are being born?
card.glance: A gray oval glow with a loose star cluster on one side, above the Teapot's spout in Sagittarius.
card.whyHere: Stars are born in clouds of gas, and the Lagoon is the rare nursery you can spot without optics, still glowing around the stars it has made.
card.see: Look about six degrees north of the tip of the Teapot's spout for a misty knot in the Milky Way. Binoculars turn it into an oval gray glow split by a dark lane, with a ragged cluster on one side and a brighter core on the other; averted vision widens the glow, and expect gray rather than pink.
card.understand: This is a cloud of hydrogen and dust where stars are still forming. A few very hot young stars flood it with ultraviolet light, and the gas glows the way the tube of a neon sign does. The dark lane that gave the Lagoon its name is dust in front of the glow, and the star knot beside it is a family the cloud has already made.
card.wonder: The light reaching you left about 4,000 to 4,600 years ago, around the age of Egypt's great pyramids.
card.connect: NGC 6530, its newborn cluster, sits right on the glow.
card.answer: The Lagoon is just such a cloud, a working nursery with its newest cluster still sitting in the gas and its brightest knot lit by a young star, Herschel 36. You are watching star formation in progress.
card.photoCaption: The ESO photograph records red hydrogen, dark dust and blue cluster stars over a long exposure; your eye sees a gray glow and a few dozen stars.
card.notSee: No pink color, no fine filaments, and no Hourglass detail at binocular power.
card.deeper: Distances come from Gaia parallaxes of its cluster NGC 6530: 1,336 (+76/−68) pc in Kuhn et al. (2019) and about 1,230 pc in Hunt & Reffert’s DR3 census. The O-type binary 9 Sagittarii supplies most of the ionizing light; the bright compact core, the Hourglass, is lit by the young O7 star Herschel 36, and the binary HD 165052 adds to the outer glow (Tothill et al. 2008). Hodierna recorded the nebula before 1654 (SEDS).

card.question: What does a family of stars look like before it leaves its birth cloud?
card.glance: A ragged knot of a dozen or more stars sitting on one side of the Lagoon's glow.
card.whyHere: The Lagoon's glow and its cluster are two faces of one event, and NGC 6530 is the family side: hundreds of siblings still sitting where they were born.
card.see: Center the Lagoon and look at the half away from its brightest patch, where a loose group of stars sits on the glow. 10×50s show a dozen or more, with fainter ones flickering in and out, so compare that side with the bright, star-poor patch across the dark lane.
card.understand: These stars formed together from the gas still glowing around them, mostly one to three million years ago, and many faint ones are still settling into steady adult life. Gaia can measure how they move, and the group is slowly spreading: as the gas is lost, gravity can no longer hold every sibling. Oddly, the spread runs mostly along one direction, not the simple outward rush astronomers expected.
card.wonder: Its brightest members will be gone within a few million years, while its smallest will still be shining long after the Sun has died.
card.connect: M21, a short hop north, is a few million years older and already out of its cloud.
card.answer: Much like NGC 6530, a ragged knot of young stars still sitting on the glowing gas that made them, about 680 known siblings weighing over 2,000 Suns together and already beginning to drift apart.
card.photoCaption: The long exposure shows hot blue cluster stars against red hydrogen; binoculars show the stars and a faint gray glow.
card.deeper: Gaia DR2 gives 1,336 (+76/−68) pc (Kuhn et al. 2019) and Gaia DR3 1,230 pc (Hunt & Reffert 2024). Gaia-ESO radial velocities plus Gaia proper motions for about 900 stars show the cluster expanding, mostly along one axis — not the simple outward rush expected if gas loss alone had unbound it (Wright et al. 2019). Hunt & Reffert count 680 Gaia members and about 2,300 solar masses; their age fit (≈4 Myr) is older than spectroscopic estimates of 1–3 Myr (Tothill et al. 2008).

card.question: What does a star nursery less than a million years old look like?
card.glance: A short, bright bar of gray light with a faint hook at one end.
card.whyHere: On this stretch of the Milky Way the Omega is the youngest nursery of all, its heaviest stars born less than a million years ago.
card.see: Sweep less than half a binocular field north of the Sagittarius Star Cloud, M24. Look for a small elongated glow, brighter than you expect, like a chalk streak; under a dark sky a fainter curl appears at one end, giving the swan or check-mark shape, and a nebula filter helps.
card.understand: Behind the bright bar sits a cluster of very massive newborn stars, mostly hidden by dust. Their ultraviolet light makes the surrounding hydrogen glow so intensely that the patch looks almost sharp-edged even in binoculars. Its age comes from a clever clock: several heavy stars have already been flung out by close encounters, and tracing their flight backward shows how recently they left.
card.wonder: Stars this heavy live only a few million years, so this whole display is a brief flash in the Galaxy's history.
card.connect: M18, just south, is a family from the same arm that lost its cloud long ago.
card.answer: It looks like the Omega, a bright, sharp-edged bar of glowing gas lit by massive stars still hidden in dust, all less than a million years old, a nursery with the lights just switched on.
card.photoCaption: The VST photograph shows pink hydrogen and dust swirls that the eye cannot see; binoculars show the bright gray bar.
card.notSee: No pink color, no dust swirls; the embedded cluster stays hidden.
card.deeper: The distance was long debated (about 1.3–2.9 kpc). A water-maser parallax gave about 2.0 kpc; Gaia astrometry of cluster stars now favors about 1.7 kpc (Kuhn et al. 2019; Stoop et al. 2024). Stoop et al. find eight O-type members of the cluster NGC 6618 and six O-type runaways whose flight times of about 0.1–0.75 Myr set a lower limit on its age. De Chéseaux discovered it in 1745–46 (SEDS).

card.question: How do newborn stars destroy the cloud that made them?
card.glance: A small, bright scatter of stars wrapped in a faint haze, north of the Sagittarius Star Cloud.
card.whyHere: Star birth is not a gentle affair, and the Eagle Nebula, home of the Pillars of Creation, shows newborn stars eating away their own birth cloud.
card.see: Sweep north from the Sagittarius Star Cloud past M17 into Serpens. M16 shows as a tight scatter of a dozen or so stars in a soft glow, and averted vision under a dark sky brings out a dim haze, brighter on one side; the pillars themselves are far too small and faint for binoculars.
card.understand: The cluster is a few million years old, and its hottest stars flood the cloud with ultraviolet light, making the gas glow and slowly boiling it away. Dense knots resist longest and are left standing as dark columns, like sandcastle towers holding out as the tide flattens the beach. Hubble photographed them in 1995 and again in 2014, and the second image showed gas streaming off their surfaces.
card.wonder: The tallest pillar is about five light-years long, more than the distance from the Sun to the nearest star.
card.connect: M17, its southern neighbor, is an even younger nursery, brighter in binoculars.
card.answer: They do it with light, their ultraviolet glare boiling the gas away until only the densest knots survive as the Pillars of Creation, and even those are fraying. Stars still form inside them, racing to finish before their cradle is gone.
card.photoCaption: ESO’s mosaic shows red hydrogen and the dark pillars; binoculars show the cluster and, at best, a faint glow.
card.notSee: The pillars, the red color and the eagle shape are photographic only.
card.deeper: Gaia DR2 parallaxes give 1,740 (+130/−120) pc for the cluster NGC 6611 (Kuhn et al. 2019). Hunt & Reffert’s Gaia DR3 fit gives about 6 Myr with a wide range; ESA/Hubble quotes about 5.5 Myr, and runaway O stars traced back to the cluster suggest a very young core. Hubble imaged the pillars in 1995 and again in high definition in 2014, revealing gas streaming off their surfaces (ESA/Hubble heic1501; NASA gives a height of about 5 light-years).

card.question: How deep into our Galaxy can binoculars actually see?
card.glance: A bright, grainy cloud of countless faint stars, about the size of a binocular field.
card.whyHere: Toward the Galaxy's center dust hides almost everything, but here a gap opens, and the view runs deeper than anywhere else in the summer Milky Way.
card.see: Look about seven degrees north of the Teapot's lid for a bright knot in the Milky Way, visible to the naked eye. Binoculars break it into a dense, sparkling sheet of faint stars with dark notches around its edges, and as your gaze drifts, tiny knots, chains and dark blotches appear.
card.understand: The glow is the combined light of countless stars too faint to see one by one, packed along a crowded stretch of a spiral arm. How far away are they? Hubble's sharp view of the same patch resolved those stars, and their faintness places them 10,000 to 16,000 light-years away, far beyond the dust that hides the rest of this direction.
card.wonder: The window is about 600 light-years wide, and its starlight set out at least 10,000 years ago, around the end of the last Ice Age.
card.connect: M18, on its northern edge, is a far nearer cluster seen against this backdrop.
card.answer: Through this hole in the dust you are looking at a slice of another spiral arm, and every grain of that glow is a distant sun.
card.photoCaption: The survey photograph shows the star cloud framed by dark dust; binoculars show the same sparkle at lower contrast.
card.deeper: M24 is not a cluster but a clear line of sight. NASA’s Hubble Messier pages put it about 10,000 light-years away, with the visible stars spread over 10,000–16,000 ly, and the window about 600 ly wide. It contains the more distant open cluster NGC 6603, and the dark nebulae Barnard 92 and 93 sit on its northern edge (SEDS). Angelo Secchi called it “Delle Caustiche” for its curving chains of stars.

card.question: How can you see a cloud that gives off no light at all?
card.glance: A dark, pipe-shaped gap in the bright Milky Way, best with the naked eye or wide binoculars under a dark sky.
card.whyHere: Before a nursery glows it is just cold, dark gas, and the Pipe Nebula is such a cloud, the nearest raw material for stars in this part of the sky.
card.see: Start at Antares and look east toward the bright heart of the Milky Way. Under a truly dark sky the naked eye shows a dark stem with a bowl at its eastern end; sweep slowly along it at low power and the background stars thin out abruptly, but you need a moonless, transparent night.
card.understand: The Pipe is cold gas laced with dust, far nearer than the stars behind it. Dust grains absorb and scatter starlight, so the cloud shows as a dark shape against the crowded center of our Galaxy. Astronomers find its distance by checking which stars it reddens: those in front shine clean, while those behind look dimmed and reddened.
card.wonder: At about 600 light-years it is seven to ten times nearer than the glowing nurseries of Sagittarius, yet you see it only as an absence of light.
card.connect: The Lagoon shows a cloud like this after its stars have switched on.
card.answer: You see its shadow: the Pipe's dust blocks the crowded Milky Way behind it, so it appears as a dark stem and bowl. Clouds like this are where stars begin, though this one has so far made only a few.
card.photoCaption: ESO’s photograph of Barnard 59 shows dust blocking a dense star field and a faint glow from a few newborn stars; binoculars show only the darkness.
card.notSee: The smoky detail and the young stars inside B59 need a telescope and a camera.
card.deeper: Distances to dark clouds come from the reddening of stars in front of and behind them. Zucker et al. (2020) place B59 at 180 (+5/−7) pc; ESO quotes 600–700 light-years. B59, the mouthpiece at the stem’s western end, is the only part of the Pipe forming stars at a noticeable rate, and even there the rate is low (ESO eso1233).

card.question: How can you tell that a star cluster is only a few million years old?
card.glance: A tight, sparkling knot of bright blue-white stars just above Scorpius's tail.
card.whyHere: Heavy stars live fast and die young, so a family still full of them must be very young, and NGC 6231 is packed with some of the heaviest stars you can see.
card.see: Follow Scorpius's tail down to the naked-eye pair ζ¹ and ζ² Scorpii, then go half a degree north to a compact knot of a dozen bright stars over fainter ones. Compare the two ζ stars, one orange and one blue-white: the orange one is a nearer foreground star, while the blue-white one belongs to this family.
card.understand: Most of the bright stars here are of the hottest, heaviest kind, which burn their fuel furiously and last only a few million years. Seeing so many still shining is like finding a room full of lit matches: someone must have struck them very recently. The birth cloud is already gone, blown away by the light and winds of these same stars.
card.wonder: X-ray telescopes, which spot young stars by their restless magnetic activity, found more than 2,000 members hidden among the field stars.
card.connect: M6, farther up the tail, is a family about ten times older.
card.answer: Its heaviest stars give it away, since they cannot last long and NGC 6231 is still full of them, so the family is only about 4 million years old.
card.photoCaption: The survey image shows the compact core of bright stars; binoculars show the same knot, with a hint of blue-white color.
card.deeper: Kuhn et al. (2017) combined Chandra X-ray and infrared data: 2,148 probable members, a distance of 1.59 kpc and ages spread over roughly 2–7 Myr. Gaia DR3 gives 1,553 pc and about 4 Myr (Hunt & Reffert 2024). NGC 6231 is the core of the Sco OB1 association. ζ¹ Sco, a blue hypergiant, is a member; orange ζ² Sco is a foreground giant far nearer to us (SIMBAD parallaxes).

card.question: Why is one star in this young cluster orange?
card.glance: A bright, scattered cluster shaped like a butterfly with open wings, an orange star on one wingtip.
card.whyHere: M6 is a family in early adulthood, about 50 million years old, and one of its members has already grown old.
card.see: From Shaula, the stinger of Scorpius, go about five degrees north. The Butterfly Cluster fills a modest part of a 7° field, two loose wings spreading from a central body, and on one wingtip BM Scorpii glows clearly orange among blue-white members; defocus slightly to make the color pop.
card.understand: All these stars were born together, so the orange one is a sibling of the blue-white ones, only heavier. Heavier stars squeeze their cores harder, burn faster and run out of core hydrogen first, then swell into cool, luminous giants. In a family this age only the most massive members have got that far, so that single orange star is a timestamp.
card.wonder: BM Scorpii is restless, slowly brightening and fading over roughly two years.
card.connect: M7, a few degrees south-east, is bigger, brighter and older.
card.answer: It was the heaviest sibling: BM Scorpii ran out of core hydrogen first and swelled into an orange giant, and its stage of life dates M6 at about 50 million years.
card.photoCaption: The survey photograph shows the scattered blue-white members and the orange giant; binoculars show the color difference clearly.
card.deeper: Hunt & Reffert (2024) fit 974 Gaia DR3 members: 452 pc, logAge 7.72 (about 30–90 Myr) and ~1,300 solar masses. BM Sco is a K2.5 Ib star listed in the GCVS as a semiregular variable (SRd, period ~815 d, V 6.8–8.7). Hodierna recorded the cluster before 1654 (SEDS).

card.question: What changes in a family of stars as it ages?
card.glance: A big, bright spray of stars, easy to the naked eye, more than a degree across.
card.whyHere: M7 is close enough to show dozens of stars with almost no magnification and old enough to have lost its brightest members, which makes it the perfect older sibling to M6.
card.see: From Shaula, go about five degrees north-east; Ptolemy's Cluster lies a few degrees south-east of the Butterfly Cluster. It is a bright patch to the naked eye, and binoculars turn it into dozens of stars over more than a degree on a rich Milky Way background, with chains, pairs and a yellowish star near the middle.
card.understand: Ptolemy's Cluster is about three times older than the Butterfly Cluster and much nearer. Its heaviest stars have finished their lives, so its brightest survivors are a little less massive, and one has become a yellow giant. Sweep the two clusters together and you compare two family photos taken at different ages.
card.wonder: The light you see left around the year 1100, about a thousand years after Ptolemy recorded it as a little cloud following the Scorpion's sting.
card.connect: NGC 6397, in Ara, is an ancient swarm dozens of times older.
card.answer: Its heaviest stars die off first: Ptolemy's Cluster, about 170 million years old, has lost its brightest blue members and now shows a yellow giant among its survivors.
card.photoCaption: ESO’s photograph shows hundreds of faint background stars that binoculars blend into the Milky Way glow; the bright members look much the same.
card.deeper: Gaia DR3 puts M7 at 276 pc with about 1,400 members and ~2,400 solar masses (Hunt & Reffert 2024). Their age fit is about 170 Myr (16–84%: 110–330 Myr); older isochrone work gave about 220 Myr (SEDS). Ptolemy described it around 130 CE as the nebula following the sting of Scorpius, and al-Sufi observed it around 964 (SEDS).

card.question: What will the young nurseries of Sagittarius look like in 200 million years?
card.glance: A rich, even scatter of faint stars about the size of the full Moon, in a busy Milky Way field.
card.whyHere: The Lagoon's newborn family will not stay young, and M23, a mature family a couple of hundred million years old, is a glimpse of its future.
card.see: From μ Sagittarii, hop about four and a half degrees north-west. M23 is a broad, slightly elongated cloud of faint stars with a brighter star off one edge, crossed by curving chains, and averted vision brings out many more members than a direct stare.
card.understand: There is no glowing gas here and no brilliant blue stars: M23's heaviest members finished their lives long ago, leaving many ordinary stars of similar brightness. Gaia counts over a thousand members, together weighing about 4,000 Suns. Its age is less certain than it looks, since two good methods disagree noticeably.
card.wonder: Its light left about 2,300 years ago, around the time of Alexander the Great.
card.connect: IC 4756, in Serpens, is a family that has held together far longer.
card.answer: They should come to look like M23, with no gas and no blue giants, just a broad, even scatter of ordinary siblings that have quietly outlived their brightest kin, provided they stay together that long.
card.photoCaption: The survey photograph shows many faint members that binoculars render as a fine glow behind the brighter stars.
card.deeper: Hunt & Reffert (2024): 713 pc, logAge 8.35 (about 140–340 Myr), 1,128 Gaia DR3 members and ~4,100 solar masses within the Jacobi radius. Cantat-Gaudin et al. (2020) give an older ~380 Myr, so “a few hundred million years” is the honest summary.

card.question: How can one pulsing star in a cluster help measure the Universe?
card.glance: A bright, loose cluster of a few dozen stars with a couple of yellowish members.
card.whyHere: Cepheids are rungs on the cosmic distance ladder, and M25 holds one inside a cluster, exactly what you need to calibrate them.
card.see: From μ Sagittarii, hop about four and a half degrees east-north-east. M25 is a loose group of bright stars over half a degree, a central pattern with scattered outliers, and U Sagittarii is one of the central stars, so compare it with its neighbors on several nights and watch it change.
card.understand: U Sgr is a Cepheid, a yellow supergiant that swells and shrinks, its brightness rising and falling every 6.7 days, and for Cepheids a longer period means a more luminous star. To turn that rule into a ruler you need Cepheids whose distance you already know. A cluster provides it, because hundreds of members give a distance far more reliable than any single star's.
card.wonder: At peak, U Sagittarii shines a little more than twice as bright as at its faintest, and a full cycle fits in a week.
card.connect: NGC 6087 in Norma hosts another cluster Cepheid.
card.answer: M25 supplies U Sagittarii's distance, and with it the star's true brightness, which calibrates the rule linking period to power. That same rule then measures the distances to other galaxies.
card.photoCaption: The survey photograph shows the cluster’s brighter members; binoculars show the same pattern, and U Sgr changing from night to night.
card.deeper: The GCVS lists U Sgr as a classical Cepheid with P = 6.745 d and V = 6.28–7.15. Cluster Cepheids anchor the period–luminosity relation because the cluster supplies an independent distance and age; Gaia DR3 puts M25 at 645 pc and about 100 Myr (Hunt & Reffert 2024). SEDS notes its importance for the Cepheid distance scale.

card.question: How can a star cluster check a Cepheid's rhythm?
card.glance: A modest cluster gathered around a bright yellowish star in the rich Norma Milky Way.
card.whyHere: One calibrator is never enough, and NGC 6087 in Norma holds another Cepheid, S Normae, to test the rule against.
card.see: From η Arae, sweep about four degrees west into Norma. NGC 6087 shows a dozen or more stars around S Normae, the brightest and slightly yellow; over a week or two, compare S Nor with its neighbors and it changes by nearly a factor of two.
card.understand: S Normae is a young, heavy supergiant passing through a brief yellow, pulsing phase of its life, with a period of nearly ten days. Its fellow cluster members share its distance and age, and those can be measured from the cluster as a whole. That lets astronomers ask a sharp question: does the period really predict the true brightness?
card.wonder: Only heavy stars crossing a narrow band of temperatures pulse like this, and only for a short stretch of their lives.
card.connect: NGC 6067, nearby, hosts Cepheids too.
card.answer: The siblings fix S Normae's distance, and its ten-day beat turns out to match the power the rule predicts, which is why Cepheids can be trusted far beyond our Galaxy.
card.photoCaption: The survey photograph shows S Nor as the brightest star near the center; in binoculars it looks faintly yellow.

card.question: How rich can an open cluster be?
card.glance: A small, bright, grainy fan of light in Scutum, almost like a globular, with a bright star at its tip.
card.whyHere: Most open clusters are loose groups of a few hundred stars, and M11 is the great exception, so rich that it is often mistaken for a globular.
card.see: Follow Aquila's tail south into little Scutum, then go about two degrees south-east of β Scuti. M11 is a compact, fan-shaped haze with a brighter star at its apex, set in the bright Scutum star cloud; in 10×50s it looks granular, and more magnification breaks it into stars.
card.understand: Most open clusters hold a few hundred stars; M11 holds thousands, born together a few hundred million years ago and still packed densely. Gaia weighs it at about 13,000 Suns, enough to rival the smallest globular clusters. Its age is less settled than its weight, with estimates from about 130 to over 300 million years.
card.wonder: Its light left over 7,000 years ago, before the first cities were built.
card.connect: M26, nearby, is a much sparser family.
card.answer: Rich enough that thousands of stars crowd into one tight fan, and their combined light makes the grainy glow you see. A V of brighter stars in it reminded an early observer of wild ducks in flight, which is how it got its name.
card.photoCaption: ESO’s image resolves thousands of stars; binoculars merge them into a grainy glow with a few brighter points.
card.deeper: Gaia DR3 gives 2,233 pc, 1,911 members above its detection limit and about 13,000 solar masses (Hunt & Reffert 2024). Ages differ by method: about 310 Myr from Cantat-Gaudin et al. (2020), at least 250 Myr per ESO, but only about 130 Myr from Hunt & Reffert’s neural-network fit. Gottfried Kirch discovered it in 1681 and William Derham resolved it in 1733; the “Wild Duck” name comes from a V of bright stars like a flock in flight (ESO eso1430).

card.question: Can a family of stars survive for nearly a billion years?
card.glance: A large, loose cloud of faint stars, a full degree across, that wants low power and a wide field.
card.whyHere: Most clusters dissolve long before they reach a billion years, so IC 4756, still together after nearly that long, is a survivor worth meeting.
card.see: From θ Serpentis, at the tip of the snake's tail, sweep about four degrees west. IC 4756 is a broad scatter of faint stars over two full-Moon widths whose edges blend into the Milky Way, so let your eyes find the slightly denser middle; NGC 6633 sits just across the border in Ophiuchus.
card.understand: Every time a cluster passes a giant gas cloud or feels the Galaxy's tides, a few stars are tugged away, so most families dissolve within a few hundred million years. IC 4756's heaviest stars are long gone, and a handful of members are now yellow and orange giants. It survived because it was born rich enough for its own gravity to hold on.
card.wonder: When this family was born, no plant had yet grown on the Earth's bare continents, and nearly all life was too small to see.
card.connect: NGC 6633, just west, is a neighbor of similar age.
card.answer: A rich one can, and IC 4756, about 840 million years old, still holds over 700 members, thinned but together.
card.photoCaption: The survey photograph shows the loose spread of members against the Milky Way; binoculars give a similar, wider impression.
card.deeper: Hunt & Reffert (2024) give 467 pc, logAge 8.92 (16–84%: 8.74–9.13) and 718 Gaia members; SIMBAD lists Gaia-era distances of 470–510 pc. Cantat-Gaudin et al. (2020) find a similar age, about 1.3 Gyr.

card.question: What does an ancient city of stars look like up close?
card.glance: A big, round, bright ball of light just above the Teapot's lid, one of the best globular clusters in binoculars.
card.whyHere: M22 is one of the nearest and brightest globular clusters, a city of stars from the Milky Way's youth, and probably the first globular anyone ever found.
card.see: From Kaus Borealis, the top of the Teapot's lid, move about two and a half degrees north-east. M22 is a bright, slightly oval glow, brighter in the middle and fading smoothly outward; brace the binoculars and compare it with nearby M28, the same kind of object with a very different apparent size.
card.understand: A globular cluster is a tight swarm of hundreds of thousands of stars held by their own gravity. These formed about 12.5 billion years ago and orbit high above and below the Galaxy's disk. The big, short-lived stars burned out long ago, so what shines now are old red giants and stars like the Sun.
card.wonder: Radio astronomers found two black holes in it, each roughly 10 to 20 times the Sun's mass, remains of its first, heaviest stars.
card.connect: M54, a few hops south, is a globular that came from another galaxy.
card.answer: It looks like M22, a bright, round glow whose edges begin to break into separate suns in binoculars, the first hint of the crowd inside. Abraham Ihle stumbled on it in 1665 while following Saturn.
card.photoCaption: The survey photograph resolves thousands of stars; binoculars show a smooth glowing ball with, at most, a grainy edge.
card.notSee: Individual stars and the tiny planetary nebula inside it are telescope targets.

(2013) derive 12.5 ± 0.5 Gyr, and Harris lists [Fe/H] = −1.70, about 1/50 of the Sun’s iron. Strader et al. (2012) identified two accreting black holes of about 10–20 solar masses with the VLA and estimated the cluster could hold 5–100 more. M22 is one of only four globulars known to contain a planetary nebula (NASA).

card.question: Does the cluster beside Antares lie anywhere near it?
card.glance: A large, soft, round glow just west of bright orange Antares; both fit in one binocular field.
card.whyHere: M4, right beside Antares, is the nearest globular cluster to us, and the pair is a perfect test of what close together in the sky really means.
card.see: Put Antares near the edge of the field and look just over a degree west. M4 is a pale, round patch, larger and dimmer-looking than you might expect, with little central brightening; under suburban skies use averted vision and keep Antares just out of view.
card.understand: Antares is a young star from a nearby group, while M4 is an ancient swarm orbiting through the Galaxy's halo. Many of its stars have already died and left white dwarfs, cooling stellar cores Hubble has seen directly. Like coals in a fire they fade at a predictable rate, so how faint the coolest have become is a clock for the cluster's age.
card.wonder: Hubble helped confirm a planet of about two and a half Jupiter masses here, orbiting a pulsar and a white dwarf: a world far older than Earth.
card.connect: NGC 6397, low in Ara, is another ancient cluster whose dead stars keep time.
card.answer: M4 lies about ten times farther than Antares, an 11.5-billion-year-old swarm that only lines up with the young star from where we stand.
card.photoCaption: The survey photograph resolves M4’s stars; binoculars show only a soft, grainy disk.

(2004) fit the white-dwarf cooling sequence at about 12.1 Gyr with a 95% lower limit of 10.3 Gyr. The planet PSR B1620−26 b orbits a pulsar–white-dwarf binary near the core (NASA). Dust in front of M4 makes it look dimmer than its distance suggests.

card.question: How can dead stars tell a cluster's age?
card.glance: A bright, slightly irregular glow low in Ara, larger than most globulars in binoculars; best from southern latitudes.
card.whyHere: NGC 6397 is the second-nearest globular cluster, and its dead stars have been used as a clock for the Galaxy's youth.
card.see: From β Arae, below Scorpius' tail, sweep about three degrees north-east. NGC 6397 is a bright, irregular glow with a concentrated core and a ragged halo that looks grainy in steady 10×50s; from mid-northern latitudes it barely clears the horizon, while from the southern hemisphere it is a highlight.
card.understand: Its heavier stars have died, leaving white dwarfs, Earth-sized embers with no fuel left that simply cool. Physics says how fast such an ember fades, so the faintest ones in a cluster tell how long the cooling has gone on. Hubble stared at this cluster long enough to find white dwarfs at the very edge of detection.
card.wonder: Its stars formed when the Universe was less than a fifth of its present age.
card.connect: Its core has collapsed into a dense knot, unlike the loose look of M4.
card.answer: White dwarfs cool at a known rate, like coals after a fire, and the faintest ones in NGC 6397 have been cooling for about 11.5 billion years, so the cluster must be at least that old.
card.photoCaption: The survey photograph shows the dense core and resolved outer stars; binoculars show a bright glow with a grainy edge.
card.deeper: Hansen et al. (2007) found a white-dwarf cooling age of 11.47 ± 0.47 Gyr (95% confidence) from deep HST imaging; turnoff fits give similar or slightly older values (13.0 ± 0.25 Gyr in VandenBerg et al. 2013). Baumgardt & Vasiliev (2021) place it at 2.48 ± 0.02 kpc. Harris flags it as core-collapsed; its iron content is about 1/100 of the Sun’s ([Fe/H] = −2.02).

card.question: Can you see a star cluster that belongs to another galaxy?
card.glance: A tiny, starlike smudge near the bottom of the Teapot: small and faint, and from another galaxy.
card.whyHere: Galaxies grow by swallowing smaller ones, and M54 lets you see it happening: it belongs to a dwarf galaxy that the Milky Way is tearing apart.
card.see: From Ascella, at the bottom of the Teapot's handle, move less than two degrees west-south-west. M54 is a small, round haze like an out-of-focus star; tap the binoculars gently and compare it with real stars nearby, and the cluster stays soft.
card.understand: In 1994 astronomers counting stars behind the center of the Milky Way noticed an excess all moving together: a faint dwarf galaxy, stretched out by our Galaxy's gravity. M54 sits at its heart, perhaps its nucleus. With 1.6 million Suns' worth of stars, it is the second most massive globular around the Milky Way.
card.wonder: Its light set out roughly eight times longer ago than the light from M22, a few degrees away.
card.connect: M55, to the east, is a Milky Way globular for comparison.
card.answer: M54 is one, about 86,000 light-years away at the heart of the Sagittarius Dwarf Galaxy, which our Galaxy is swallowing right now. You look through the Milky Way's crowded center at a cluster that came from somewhere else.
card.photoCaption: The survey image shows a dense, concentrated core; binoculars show a small soft point.
card.notSee: Individual stars and the host galaxy itself are invisible; the dwarf galaxy was found statistically from star counts.
card.deeper: Ibata, Gilmore & Irwin (1994) discovered the Sagittarius dwarf spheroidal galaxy; M54 coincides with its nucleus (Bellazzini et al. 2008). Baumgardt & Vasiliev (2021) place it at 26.3 ± 0.3 kpc with 1.6 million solar masses, second only to ω Centauri among the cataloged globulars. VandenBerg et al. (2013) find 11.75 ± 0.5 Gyr.

card.question: Why does such a big cluster look so faint and ghostly?
card.glance: A large, faint, round glow low in the south, more than half the width of the full Moon, with little central brightening.
card.whyHere: Not every globular is a bright, tight ball, and M55 shows the other style: a loose, pale disk, ancient and spread out.
card.see: From Ascella, at the bottom of the Teapot's handle, sweep about eight degrees east into an empty-looking field. M55 is a broad, pale disk with almost no bright core and edges that look mottled under a dark sky; from northern latitudes it needs a clear southern horizon.
card.understand: A cluster's light is the same whether its stars are packed or spread, but spread out it covers more sky at lower intensity, like butter scraped over too much bread. M54, a few hops west, is about eight times more massive yet looks smaller and fainter, because it is about five times farther away. Size, spread and distance all shape what you see.
card.wonder: Averted vision makes it noticeably larger, because the edge of your eye's field is more sensitive to faint light.
card.connect: M75, far out in the halo, is a remote globular in the same part of the sky.
card.answer: Its stars are loosely spread, so M55's light covers a wide patch thinly and the glow looks pale and ghostly. It is also among the oldest globulars measured, about 13 billion years old.

card.question: How old are the oldest star swarms in our Galaxy?
card.glance: A bright, compact ball of light beside a faint star, in an otherwise empty patch of Serpens.
card.whyHere: M5 is one of the finest globular clusters in the sky, a swarm of a few hundred thousand stars billions of years older than the Sun.
card.see: From Unukalhai, the brightest star in the snake's head, sweep about eight degrees south-west. M5 is a round glow with a bright, almost starlike core fading into a broad halo, with a faint star just to its south; in 10×50s it can pass for a fuzzy star until you notice the halo.
card.understand: Ages come from the turnoff, the point where a cluster's stars start to leave their steady middle age: the dimmer that point, the older the cluster. M5's turnoff gives about 11.5 billion years. Its stars are also poor in heavy elements, because the gas they formed from had not yet been enriched by many generations of dying stars.
card.wonder: Hubble found young-looking blue stragglers among its ancient stars, probably rebuilt by collisions or mergers.
card.connect: The Great Hercules Cluster, its northern near-twin, lies at almost the same distance with a similar mass.
card.answer: About 11 to 12 billion years for M5 and its kind, more than twice the Sun's age, which makes them snapshots of an early, chemically simpler Milky Way.

card.question: Why do two twin clusters look so different?
card.glance: A round, evenly bright glow in the middle of Ophiuchus, with its twin M12 a few degrees away.
card.whyHere: M10 and M12 sit at almost the same distance, which turns them into a controlled experiment: any difference you see belongs to the clusters themselves.

card.understand: Both are globular clusters about 16,500 light-years away, only about a thousand light-years apart in space. M10 holds nearly twice the mass of M12 and packs its stars more tightly toward the center. That bright, dense core is what makes it look more defined in binoculars.

card.connect: M12, three degrees north-west, is the looser twin.
card.answer: It is build, not distance: the heavier, more tightly packed twin looks brighter and more compact. The two have orbited the Galaxy for more than 11 billion years and happen to be near neighbors right now.

card.question: What thins out a globular cluster over billions of years?
card.glance: A soft, round glow, larger and paler than its twin M10 a few degrees south-east.
card.whyHere: M12 is the looser twin of M10, at the same distance but with about half the mass, and the difference has a cause.

card.question: What does the Galaxy's crowded core do to a cluster that orbits near it?
card.glance: A small, bright glow with a lopsided edge, low in the south near the Scorpius–Ophiuchus border.
card.whyHere: Globular clusters crowd toward the Galaxy's center, and M62, orbiting only a few thousand light-years from the hub, shows what that neighborhood does to them.
card.see: From ε Scorpii, sweep about five degrees north-north-east, or about eight degrees east-south-east of Antares. M62 is a compact, bright glow whose brightest part sits off-center, so one side looks squashed, and nearby M19 makes a good comparison.
card.understand: Near the hub, the Galaxy pulls harder on a cluster's near side than on its far side, stretching it the way the Moon raises tides on Earth. Over many orbits that strips away outer stars. A century ago Harlow Shapley noticed how globulars crowd toward this part of the sky and used it to work out where the Galaxy's center lies.
card.wonder: Astronomers have found a black hole and many X-ray-bright star pairs in its dense core, born from close encounters between stars.
card.connect: M19, just north, is the most flattened globular known.
card.answer: It stretches and strips it: the hub's tides pull M62's outer stars away, which may explain its lopsided look.

card.question: Are all globular clusters round?
card.glance: A small, oval glow east of Antares, clearly stretched north to south.
card.whyHere: Globular clusters are usually the roundest things in the sky, which makes M19, the most flattened one known, a puzzle.

card.understand: Most globulars are nearly round, because their stars swarm in every direction. M19 lies only about 5,500 light-years from the Galaxy's center, where the hub's gravity is strong. Its shape may come from those tides, or from a slow spin of the whole cluster that flattens it the way Earth's rotation flattens our planet.
card.wonder: Its light set out about 27,000 years ago, during the last Ice Age.
card.connect: M5 in Serpens orbits far from the hub, calm and round.
card.answer: M19 is visibly stretched, the most oblate globular known, shaped by the strong gravity near the Galaxy's center or by its own slow spin.

card.question: Which cluster helps calibrate the cosmic distance scale?
card.glance: A rich, compact, granular cluster in the bright Norma star cloud.
card.whyHere: Cepheids need calibrating, and NGC 6067 in Norma is a heavyweight young cluster hosting more than one of them.
card.see: From κ Normae, look less than half a degree north. NGC 6067 is a dense, grainy patch against a crowded Milky Way, and 10×50s show a few members over a fine glow.
card.understand: It hosts Cepheids such as QZ Normae, pulsing stars whose periods reveal their true brightness. The cluster's many members supply a reliable distance, so putting the two together tests the rule that turns a Cepheid's beat into a distance. Every galaxy distance measured with Cepheids leans on checks like this one.
card.wonder: Gaia weighs it at over 7,000 Suns, one of the more massive young clusters within a few thousand light-years.
card.connect: NGC 6087, about four degrees south-south-east, has a Cepheid too.
card.answer: NGC 6067 is one, its Cepheids' periods giving their true brightness while the cluster's known distance checks the rule.

card.question: Can a single star outshine a whole cluster of stars?
card.glance: A small, bright, starlike glow roughly midway between Antares and Acrab.

They create oddities such as blue stragglers, stars rebuilt by collisions or mergers, and pairs in which a white dwarf feeds on a companion. card.understand: NGC 6520 is a family of stars about 110 million years old. Beside it, Barnard 86 is a dense clump of dust blocking the crowded star field behind. One is made of light and the other only of shadow, though dust like this is what clusters are born from.
card.wonder: Gaia places the cluster about 5,600 light-years away, so its light set out around when the first cities were rising.
card.connect: The Lagoon lies a short sweep north.
card.answer: They do here, where the cluster NGC 6520 sits beside Barnard 86, a dust clump blotting out the star clouds.

card.question: How quickly does a young cluster leave its birth cloud?
card.glance: A small, tight group of stars a short hop north of the Lagoon.
card.whyHere: M21 comes from the same star-forming region as the Lagoon, a little older and already out of its cloud.
card.see: From the Lagoon, sweep about two degrees north. M21 is a small knot of a dozen stars, and the faint Trifid Nebula lies just south-west but is hard in binoculars.
card.understand: M21 was born in the same star-forming region as the Lagoon's cluster, only a few million years earlier. Its hottest stars cleared away the leftover gas with their ultraviolet light and winds. What remains is a family still showing its youth in bright blue-white members.
card.wonder: Its light left about 3,900 years ago, when Stonehenge’s great stones had already stood for centuries.
card.connect: M23 shows what such a family becomes after a couple of hundred million years.
card.answer: Within a few million years: M21, about five million years old, has already shed its gas.

card.question: What hides in the quiet far-southern sky of Corona Australis?
card.glance: A small, bright, concentrated glow in Corona Australis.
card.whyHere: Corona Australis looks empty, but it hides a compact, ancient globular, about 12.5 billion years old.
card.see: From α Telescopii go about four degrees north-west. Look for a small, round glow with a bright core.
card.understand: Its stars formed early in the Galaxy's history. They hold less than 2% of the Sun's share of heavy elements, which are forged inside stars and spread when they die. So little enrichment means these stars formed before many generations had lived.
card.wonder: Its light left about 25,000 years ago, when ice sheets still covered much of the northern world.
card.connect: NGC 6397, larger and nearer, lies about eleven degrees south-south-west.
card.answer: It hides NGC 6541, a compact globular about 12.5 billion years old whose stars are almost free of heavy elements.

card.question: Is the small cluster in front of the star cloud part of it?
card.glance: A small, sparse sprinkle of stars between M17 and the Sagittarius Star Cloud.
card.whyHere: M18 is a small young cluster seen against the vast Sagittarius Star Cloud, a reminder that the sky is layered.
card.see: From M17, move about one degree south; M18 is a small knot of a few brighter stars. Continue south to M24 and compare the scale.
card.understand: At about 30 million years, M18 is young, yet already free of its birth cloud. Gaia puts it about 4,900 light-years away. The star cloud behind it lies about twice as far, so the two only overlap on the sky.
card.wonder: Its brightest stars were born after the dinosaurs died out.
card.connect: The Sagittarius Star Cloud, just south, opens a window to a farther spiral arm.
card.answer: M18 is a young family in the foreground, about half as far away as the star cloud it seems to touch.

card.question: Why does M28 look so much smaller than M22?
card.glance: A small, bright, round glow just north-west of the Teapot's lid.
card.whyHere: M28 is a compact globular right beside big M22, the same kind of object with a much smaller look.
card.see: From Kaus Borealis, the top of the Teapot's lid, move about one degree north-west. M28 is a small, concentrated glow, and M22 is about three degrees east-north-east.
card.understand: M28 lies over one and a half times as far as M22. It also holds only about half its mass. The first effect spreads its light thinner, the second gives it less light to spread, and together they shrink it to a small, compact glow.
card.wonder: Its light left about 17,500 years ago, around when people were painting the caves of Lascaux.
card.connect: M22 is the big, bright version.
card.answer: Distance and weight work together here, for M28 is the smaller, farther sibling of M22 and both effects push the same way.

card.question: Do all open clusters look as rich as M11?
card.glance: A small, faint, partly resolved haze in Scutum.
card.whyHere: M26 sits near rich M11, a sparse family that shows clusters come in all sizes.
card.see: From α Scuti go about two and a half degrees south-east; M26 is a tiny haze with one or two brighter stars. Use the field pattern to separate it from the rich background.
card.understand: M26 has about a fifth of M11's mass at a broadly similar distance. It is also younger, about 130 million years old. Fewer stars means a fainter, sparser glow, even though the two families formed in the same way.
card.wonder: Its light left about 6,000 years ago, before anyone had learned to write.
card.connect: M11, a few degrees north, is the rich contrast.
card.answer: M26 shows that they do not, offering only a faint haze with a couple of stars where M11 blazes with thousands.

card.question: Is this faint sprinkle near M25 a real cluster?
card.glance: A small, loose grouping of faint stars east of M25.
card.whyHere: NGC 6716 is a modest family of similar age to nearby M25, sparser and harder to pick out.
card.see: From ξ² Sagittarii, go about one and a half degrees north-west. Look for a small cluster of faint stars against the Milky Way.
card.understand: Gaia measures the distance and motion of every star in the field. About 930 of them share the same values, at roughly 2,300 light-years. That shared motion is what makes it a real cluster, about 80 million years old.
card.wonder: It formed in the age of the late dinosaurs.
card.connect: M25 is a richer family of similar age.
card.answer: It is real, and most of the family is invisible to you: of the hundreds Gaia found, binoculars catch only a sprinkle.

card.question: How far out into the halo can binoculars reach?
card.glance: A tiny, nearly starlike smudge in an empty part of Sagittarius.
card.whyHere: M75 is one of the most distant globular clusters within binocular reach, far out in the Galaxy's halo.
card.see: From Dabih (β Capricorni), go about eight degrees south-west. Expect a faint, almost starlike point that stays soft when you tap the binoculars; a steady mount helps.
card.understand: At about 67,000 light-years, M75 lies far beyond the Galaxy's center, out in the halo. It holds about 460,000 Suns' worth of stars. At that distance they shrink to a near-point, the light of nearly half a million suns reduced to a faint smudge.
card.wonder: Its light set out about 67,000 years ago, when our own species still lived mostly in Africa.
card.connect: M55, nearer, looks much larger.
card.answer: To M75, a soft point far beyond the Galaxy's center and one of the most distant globulars binoculars can reach.

edge.NGC6530>M23: Fast-forward about two hundred million years, let the gas disperse and the brightest blue stars die, and a family like {prev} comes to look like {next}.
edge.M21>M23: From a family about five million years old to one about forty times older, a few degrees away: the same kind of birth, a much later chapter.
edge.M8>M24: From one nursery to the crowded Galaxy behind it: about six degrees north, a gap in the dust opens onto the spiral arm beyond.
edge.M17>M16: Next door, the same process is at work in another cloud lit from inside by newborn heavy stars, this one carved into the famous pillars.
Like {prev}, {next} glows because young, very hot stars energize the cloud they were born in.
edge.M17>M8: The Lagoon is lit the same way as the Omega, by hot young stars energizing their birth cloud, though here the cluster is already in view.
edge.M17>M18: One degree south, on the same spiral arm, lies a family about forty times older, its cloud long gone and only the stars remaining.
edge.M16>M42: The winter sky's great nursery works exactly like {prev}, with newborn heavy stars lighting the cloud that made them.
edge.M18>M24: {prev} sits in front of {next}, about half as far away as the star cloud it seems to touch.

edge.DN-Pipe>M8: The Pipe is cold dust before its stars switch on, and the Lagoon shows what such a cloud becomes once newborn stars light it up.
From a cloud you can see only as a shadow to one glowing with its own young stars.
edge.DN-Pipe>M24: The Pipe is dust blocking the Galaxy's light, and the star cloud is its opposite, a rare gap in the dust where the crowded disk shines through.
edge.DN-Pipe>DN-BarnardE: Barnard's E in Aquila is another dark cloud, seen only by the starlight it blocks.
edge.DN-Pipe>STAR-Antares: In the same corner of the sky sit cold, dark raw material for stars and a star near the end of its life.
edge.NGC6231>M6: Up Scorpius's tail lies a family about ten times older, its heaviest stars gone and one member already turned into an orange giant.
From a few million years to about fifty million, a chance to see what age does to a family of stars.
edge.M6>M7: A few degrees south-east lies a family about three times older and much nearer, its brightest survivor now a yellow giant.
Two clusters in one sweep and two ages, {prev} the younger family and {next} the older one.
edge.NGC6231>M7: Both are families of stars in Scorpius's tail, but {next} is about forty times older and nearly six times closer.
edge.NGC6124>NGC6231: Five degrees east lies a cluster about twenty times younger, still packed with its heaviest stars.
edge.NGC6231>STAR-Antares: Antares comes from a nearby group of young stars, while NGC 6231 is a young family about ten times farther away.
edge.M7>IC4651: Farther south in Ara lies a family roughly ten times older than M7 that has somehow held together.
edge.M7>NGC6397: From a loose family under two hundred million years old to an ancient ball of stars more than sixty times older.
edge.M4>NGC6397: Hubble has counted the dead stars of both of the nearest globulars, and in each the faintest white dwarfs act as a clock for the cluster's age.
Like {prev}, {next} has been dated by how far its white dwarfs have cooled.
edge.M4>M80: About four degrees apart and both globulars, yet {next} lies more than five times farther away, so it shrinks to a small, bright smudge.
edge.M80>M14: Both clusters have hosted a nova, T Scorpii in 1860 and a fainter one in M14 in 1938.
edge.M22>M28: Three degrees apart and the same kind of object, yet {next} looks much smaller, because it is over one and a half times as far and about half as massive.
edge.M22>M54: From one of our nearest globulars to one that belongs to another galaxy, {next}, about eight times farther away.
Step outside the Milky Way: {next} arrived with a dwarf galaxy that our Galaxy is now swallowing.
edge.M54>M55: {next} looks bigger and brighter, yet {prev} holds about eight times the mass, and the difference is distance, about five times.
Looking big is not the same as being big, for a nearer, lighter cluster can outshine a heavier, distant one.
edge.M55>M75: Out to the far halo, where M75 lies nearly four times farther than M55 and shrinks to a near-point.
edge.M22>M24: From a halo globular to the Galaxy's crowded disk: the star cloud is a slice of spiral arm, and the globular a visitor from above it.
edge.M10>M12: Same distance, same kind of cluster, three degrees apart, yet {next} carries about half the mass of {prev} and looks looser and dimmer.
edge.M12>M14: M14 is more than five times heavier than M12 but nearly twice as far away, so it looks fainter.
edge.M62>M19: Four degrees north lies another globular orbiting close to the Galaxy's hub, this one stretched into an oval.
edge.M9>M62: M62 is another of the globulars crowding toward the Galaxy's center, the very pattern Harlow Shapley used a century ago to locate that center.
edge.M4>M62: From the nearest globular to one deep inside the Galaxy, about three times farther and close to the hub.
edge.M12>M19: Heading south, the globulars crowd together toward the Galaxy's center, the clue Harlow Shapley used to find where the center lies.
edge.M5>M13: The Great Hercules Cluster is M5's northern near-twin, at almost the same distance and with a similar mass of ancient stars.
edge.M5>M4: Both are ancient globulars of similar age, but M4 lies about four times nearer.
edge.NGC6397>NGC6541: Eleven degrees north lies a globular of similar age, three times farther away.
edge.M25>NGC6087: NGC 6087 is another young family hosting a Cepheid, where S Normae pulses every ten days to U Sagittarii's six and three-quarters.
edge.NGC6087>NGC6067: Four degrees north lies a richer family with Cepheids of its own: the same physics, another yardstick.
edge.NGC6167>NGC6134: A degree apart in Norma, NGC 6134 is many times older than NGC 6167 by Gaia's estimate.
edge.IC4651>NGC6208: Two survivors in Ara, both well over a billion years old, which makes them rare among open clusters.
edge.NGC5822>NGC6124: From a billion-year-old family to one about thirteen times younger.
edge.M11>M26: In the same corner of the Milky Way and at a broadly similar distance, {prev} weighs about five times more than {next}, a rich family and a poor one side by side.
edge.M11>IC4756: IC 4756 is nearly five times nearer than M11 and older, so its stars spread wide instead of crowding into a glow.
edge.IC4756>NGC6633: Just west, across the Ophiuchus border, lies another loose family from a similar era, and together they make a classic binocular pair.
edge.M23>IC4756: IC 4756 is a few times older again, nearly a billion years, and still holding together.
edge.M25>NGC6716: NGC 6716 is a sparser family of about the same age and distance as M25.
edge.M9>NGC6520: Both sit beside dark dust clouds that dim the starlight behind them.
edge.NGC6530>NGC6231: NGC 6231 is a family of heavy young stars a little further along than {prev}, its birth cloud already blown away.
edge.DN-Pipe>M16: The Pipe is a whole dark cloud before its stars switch on, while the Eagle's pillars are the last dense scraps of a cloud its stars are destroying.
edge.M6>STAR-Antares: BM Scorpii in M6 and Antares tell the same story on different scales: heavy stars that ran low on core hydrogen and swelled into cool, luminous giants.
edge.M25>NGC6067: NGC 6067 is another cluster with resident Cepheids, pulsing stars whose cluster supplies the distance that calibrates them.
edge.M25>HR7020: δ Scuti pulses too, but in a few hours rather than days, a smaller, hotter star with a faster rhythm.
edge.NGC6087>NGC6208: From a young family with a pulsing yellow supergiant to a sparse survivor over a billion years old.
edge.M11>M23: The two are of similar age, but M11 weighs about three times as much as M23 and lies about three times as far.
edge.M55>NGC6397: Both are among the oldest globulars measured, around 12 to 13 billion years old, and both are very poor in heavy elements.
edge.M5>M3: M3 in Canes Venatici is another bright globular of similar mass, the spring sky's counterpart to M5.
edge.M10>M14: M14 holds about three times M10's mass yet looks fainter, because it is nearly twice as far away.
edge.M19>M9: M9 is another globular crowding toward the Galaxy's center, this one dimmed by a dust cloud in front of it.
